articles.title: I used to think I was an ambivalent mother, then my child started to stutter | Bridie Jabour
articles.summary: I snapped at my children. Resented daily pickup. But I was there when he needed me, and my perception of myself completely changed. I still can’t pinpoint when it happened, but it felt as though my child lost the ability to communicate overnight.
body: Of course, that is not what happened, and he never lost the ability to communicate. But it felt as though he did at the time. And even with the benefit of hindsight, it felt like he went from a chatty three-year-old to being unable to get a sentence out. “W-w-w-w-w-w-w-w-w-what c-c-c-c-c-c-c-c-c-c-can I-I-I-I-I-I-I” and then silence as he gave up trying and just looked up at me.

I often joke my parenting approach is one of benign neglect, and that I lack any instinct at all. I still do lean into that caricature at times (“I will have to do a few minutes of parenting this weekend,” I recently texted the family group chat in mock horror). This joke originated when I first became a mother more than eight years ago. I perpetuated this idea that my children were not the centre of my world and therefore I was somehow different from other mothers.
Privately I thought I was more ambivalent about motherhood than I anticipated. It turns out I had mistaken what maternal ambivalence was.
points: But I was there when he needed me, and my perception of myself completely changed.
I still can’t pinpoint when it happened, but it felt as though my child lost the ability to communicate overnight.

articles.title: Samsung's Frame Pro isn't just a gorgeous TV, it opened my eyes to art
articles.summary: The design-forward TV delivers a performance that few in the category can – while attracting compliments as wall decor. Can’t hear what’s playing on TV? It’s not your ears, it’s the flat screen. These affordable soundbars can help.
body: When they are screening blockbusters, huge TVs are cinematic portals to another world. When they’re off, huge TVs are hideous black mirrors. Samsung has always understood this home decor landmine and aimed to defuse it in 2017 with The Frame, the first-ever “art TV”: a television disguised as a framed painting.

As a female tech editor who spent years appraising the banal designs of 1990s tech, I can palpably remember how thrilled I was to see this innovative melding of form and function, which seemed like a novel luxury at the time. Fast-forward nearly a decade, and Samsung’s pricey niche concept has gone decisively mainstream, with competition from LG, Hisense, TCL and even Amazon.
But Samsung hasn’t been sitting still: The Frame Pro boasts cordless architecture, a matte screen and customizable magnetic bezels.
points: The design-forward TV delivers a performance that few in the category can – while attracting compliments as wall decor.

articles.title: I thought I was too broken for sex. Here’s how I found pleasure again
articles.summary: I was forced to examine the idea of sexual pleasure after a tumor was removed from my spinal cord. Ten years ago, my right elbow started to hurt. The internet suggested I had tennis elbow, so I stopped playing tennis.
body: For good measure, I consulted an occupational therapist about my nightly bullet-vibrator routine after reading that golfer’s elbow is common among construction workers who operate heavy-duty vibrating machinery. He listened closely and said he’d note VRI on my patient chart. I asked what VRI meant, eager to end my diagnostic journey. “Vibrator-related injury,” he responded. We busted out laughing.

After three years, weak hands and shaky legs had joined the elbow pain. None of the diagnoses I researched or received (a pinched ulnar nerve, tendinitis and thoracic outlet syndrome) fully explained my symptoms. Eventually, an MRI found a tumor growing inside my spinal cord. One surgeon estimated that without treatment, my body would undergo complete, permanent paralysis from the neck down within a year.

articles.title: What did I learn in the kitchen this week? The longer it takes to cook, the less you want to eat it | Adrian Chiles
articles.summary: After grilling, skinning, chopping and stirring, stirring, stirring, my feelings towards my favourite Balkan relish, ajvar, changed. Those Macedonian nans must be made of girders.
body: I f you ever meet someone from North Macedonia and find yourself short of conversation, then one word will get things going nicely. That word is ajvar. Pronounce it “Ivor”, as in The Engine – not quite right but it’ll do. Depending on who you ask, ajvar is a condiment, spread, sauce or relish. It’s made – also depending on who you ask – with red peppers and aubergine. You can eat it with meat, cheese, fish, vegetables, on toast or, using a large spoon, straight from the jar.

I was accompanying a 13-year-old called Ilijana as she played the British chess grandmaster Nigel Short. This was on the waterfront in Split, Croatia. Long story. All you need to know is that my contribution to the contest was zero. All I could do was try to bond with her somehow, by finding some area of common ground. So I said the magic word: ajvar! This was the conversational equivalent of a chess move – something with a knight perhaps? – which she didn’t see coming. It worked a treat. Suddenly she was all smiles, telling me how her grandma’s ajvar was the best in the world.
points: After grilling, skinning, chopping and stirring, stirring, stirring, my feelings towards my favourite Balkan relish, ajvar, changed.
Those Macedonian nans must be made of girders.

articles.title: It’s Time to Take Ranch Dressing Seriously
articles.summary: You can tell a lot about someone by the way they talk about ranch dressing. Do they express Midwestern passion for the condiment, or coastal-elite distaste? Do they limit its usage to crisp iceberg lettuce salads, or do they become a jester of pairings, drizzling the sauce over steak, pasta, and…
body: Ranch dressing was first invented in 1954 by a contractor named Steve Henson, with the original recipe consisting of buttermilk, mayonnaise, and various herbs and seasonings. Initially, Henson served the dressing to his workers to help liven up their salads; as its popularity soared, he began serving it out of a rustic, 1800s-stagecoach-turned-restaurant called Cold Spring Tavern in the Santa Ynez mountains of California, where it’s still served to this day. Early DIY packets of the sauce, which were whipped up at Henson’s Hidden Valley Ranch (yes, a real place ), were marketed as a party dip — a foreshadowing detail of its crowd-pleasing talents.

articles.title: How Doll Invasion Went From a Trans House Party to a Fire Island Mainstay
articles.summary: "It was transsexual summer camp," Doll Invasion founder Fran Tirado recalls of the now-annual Fire Island celebration and fundraiser's humble beginnings.
body: About a decade ago, I took my maiden voyage to the 31-mile stretch of sand along the southern shore of New York known as Fire Island. At the time, I didn’t know that much about the Pines. I’d heard about “tea” and the whole concept as a kind of gay guy Treasure Island for brave New Yorkers who took a train to another train, then a shuttle, then a ferry in search of known and unknown plunder.
Later, when I found myself at a RuGirl-studded pool party co-sponsored by a vodka brand and a gay dating app, I realized that people did, in fact, know this place. Just not my people.

Year after year, I’d return to the island to reprise that tradition. Then I started pitching around the concept of a “Doll Invasion.” I wanted to rent a house, book some DJs, and throw an actual party, inviting trans people—and anyone who loved trans people—to overcome the deterrent of the island’s reputation and make their own maiden voyages.
points: "It was transsexual summer camp," Doll Invasion founder Fran Tirado recalls of the now-annual Fire Island celebration and fundraiser's humble beginnings.

articles.title: The Distinctly Brazilian Flavor of São Paolo's Japanese Cuisine
articles.summary: From Nipo-Brazilian cuisine that relies on Amazonian fish to home-cooking-inspired izakayas to traditional omakase, São Paulo’s Japanese restaurants are richer and more varied than ever before.
body: At Aizomê, a stylish Japanese restaurant shrouded by a thick wall of trees just off São Paulo ’s main thoroughfare, Avenida Paulista, the food is both recognizable to devotees of Japanese cuisine and distinctly Brazilian. You might find pirarucu, an enormous Amazonian riverfish, in saikyo yaki, a traditional Japanese sweet-miso preparation more commonly used on black cod. Ponzu incorporates tucupi, a tart yellow sauce made from fermented wild manioc, a root native to the Amazon.

“I’m third generation,” says owner Telma Shiraishi, who was born and raised in São Paulo and whose grandparents hail from the Wakayama and Iwate prefectures of Japan. “It doesn’t make sense for me to make a cuisine that is 100% Japanese, bringing 100% of ingredients from Japan.”
Telma Shiraishi has led Aizomê for two decades, bringing Brazilian ingredients and Japanese techniques under one roof.
points: From Nipo-Brazilian cuisine that relies on Amazonian fish to home-cooking-inspired izakayas to traditional omakase, São Paulo’s Japanese restaurants are richer and more varied than ever before.

articles.title: All the Best Looks From the 2026 Venice Film Festival
articles.summary: As the 2026 Venice Film Festival kicks off this week, all eyes will be on the red carpet—with the likes of George and Amal Clooney, Claire Foy, and Robert Pattinson arriving in the Italian city. See all the best fashion from Venice Film Festival so far.
body: Red carpet lovers, it’s your lucky day: The 2026 Venice Film Festival has officially arrived.

The film roster for this year’s festival has plenty of buzzy projects to take in: Among them is Martin McDonagh’s Oscar-tipped black comedy Wild Horse Nine; Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime; a Robert Pattinson-led portrait of To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen; and Bunker, Florian Zeller’s marital drama starring Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem.

Better year, however, is what all of these A-listers will be wearing on the step and repeat for the splashy premieres. This is, after all, the festival that last year offered the first glimpses of new-era Chanel, Dior, Versace and Bottega Veneta before their respective runway debuts, and which has given us Lady Gaga’s feathered Valentino couture gown in 2018 and Zendaya’s wet-look Balmain dress in 2021, among other standout moments.

articles.title: 8 Best Antioxidant Serums to Protect Against Future Skin Damage
articles.summary: The best antioxidant serums use vitamin C, vitamin E, resveratrol, and other active ingredients to defend skin against external aggressors. Shop our top picks.
body: Think of the best antioxidant serums as your insurance against future damage—they supplement your first line of defense (namely, sunscreen ) in order to protect skin. These face serums can make a meaningful difference in maintaining healthy, youthful skin over the years, even if you don’t see their effects immediately. What makes them so impactful: “Every day, we’re exposed to things like UV radiation, pollution, and other environmental stressors that generate free radicals,” says Melanie Palm, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in La Jolla, California. “Those free radicals can over time contribute to pigmentation, collagen breakdown, and other signs of premature aging.”

Like a superhero of sorts, topical antioxidants help neutralize some of those free radicals, effectively taking them out of commission before they can harm skin. While that doesn’t mean you can swap out your sunscreen for a vitamin C serum, they do work in tandem. And some antioxidant serums even go above and beyond mere protection. “Vitamin C, for example, is involved in collagen synthesis and can help address uneven pigmentation, so you’re getting both preventive and corrective benefits,” says Dr. Palm.
points: The best antioxidant serums use vitamin C, vitamin E, resveratrol, and other active ingredients to defend skin against external aggressors.
